subtitle: The same query can be answered a thousand ways; the optimiser picks one. Indexes are why it can be fast.

steps.body:
You type one line of SQL and an answer appears. What happened in between? Think of a travel agent: you say where you want to go, and the agent works out the cheapest route without you asking. A query is parsed, checked and translated into relational algebra; the optimiser rewrites it into cheaper equivalents and picks an execution plan using statistics; the evaluator runs the plan.

The key rewrites are simple but powerful: push selections down before joins (fewer rows to join), push projections down, and choose the join order and the join algorithm. See the difference in numbers. R has 10 000 rows and S has 10 000 rows; a selection keeps 1% of R; join on a key. Selecting first joins 100 rows of R with S. Joining first compares 10⁴×10⁴ pairs before filtering, that is 10⁸ pairs. Why push selections below joins? Because filtering first leaves far fewer rows to combine. The optimiser sits between the algebra and the plan.
keynotes: A query is parsed, checked and translated into relational algebra; the optimiser rewrites it into cheaper equivalents and picks a plan using statistics; the evaluator runs it.
Key rewrites: push selections and projections down, and choose the join order and algorithm.
With 10 000 rows in each of R and S and a selection keeping 1% of R, selecting first handles 100 rows against 10⁸ pairs when joining first.

ind.body:
Finding a word in a book without an index means reading every page. With an index at the back, you jump straight there. Databases do exactly that. Without an index a lookup scans every block; an index is a separate structure mapping a key to record locations.

Indexes come in kinds. Dense indexes have an entry per record; sparse ones have one per block. A clustered (primary) index orders the file itself; a secondary index is on a non-ordering attribute. Count the savings. A file has 1 000 000 records, 100 per block: 10 000 blocks. A sequential scan reads 10 000 blocks, on average 5 000. A sparse index with one entry per block has 10 000 entries; binary search over them needs about log₂10 000 ≈ 14 reads, plus 1 data block, which is 15. The price of an index? Indexes speed reads and slow writes (each insert updates them) and cost space.
keynotes: An index is a separate structure mapping a key to record locations; dense indexes have an entry per record, sparse ones one per block.
A clustered (primary) index orders the file itself; a secondary index is on a non-ordering attribute.
For 1 000 000 records at 100 per block, a scan reads 10 000 blocks (5 000 on average) but a sparse index needs about 15 reads.
Indexes speed reads, slow writes and cost space.

bplus.body:
You will meet the star of database indexing here: the B+ tree: a wide, shallow balanced tree whose internal nodes hold only separator keys and whose leaves hold all the keys, linked in order for fast range queries. Why wide? Because each node is a whole disk block holding hundreds of keys, so a few hops reach the answer.

Watch an insertion of 1…7 into an order-3 tree. A B-tree ends with root key 4 and height 3, but the B+ tree keeps every key in its leaves (1 2 3 4 5 6 7). In the figure the green arrows chain the leaves for range scans, while the B-tree stores keys in internal nodes too. With hundreds of keys per node, three or four levels index billions of rows. The leaves are linked so that a range query can walk along the leaf level without climbing back up.
keynotes: A B+ tree is a wide, shallow balanced tree: internal nodes hold only separator keys and the leaves hold all keys, linked in order for range queries.
Inserting 1…7 into an order-3 tree gives a B-tree with root key 4 and height 3, while the B+ tree keeps every key (1 2 3 4 5 6 7) in its leaves.
With hundreds of keys per node, three or four levels index billions of rows.

hash.body:
What if you only ever ask “find this exact key”? Then there is an even faster trick: static hashing maps a key through h(k) to a bucket (a block or chain). Equality lookups cost about one block access. The catch: range queries are impossible, and a fixed number of buckets degrades as the file grows.

Dynamic (extendible) hashing fixes that by adding buckets on demand, using more bits of the hash. And collisions chain: keys 5, 10, 3, 8 into 5 buckets give 5|10 - - 3|8 -. See how colliding keys share a bucket in the figure. A hash index is better than a B+ tree when you only need equality lookups.
keynotes: Static hashing maps a key through h(k) to a bucket; equality lookups cost about one block access but range queries are impossible.
Dynamic (extendible) hashing adds buckets on demand by using more bits of the hash.
Keys 5, 10, 3, 8 into 5 buckets give 5|10 - - 3|8 -, with colliding keys sharing a bucket.

store.body:
Why do databases care about blocks at all? You might wonder. Because the disk is slow. Data is stored in fixed-size blocks on disk, and reading a block costs milliseconds while CPU work is nanoseconds, so a DBMS counts its cost in block accesses.

Records are organised as a heap (unordered), sequential (sorted), or hashed. Variable-length records use slotted pages, and buffer management keeps hot blocks in memory. So the cost models count mainly the number of disk block accesses.
keynotes: Data is stored in fixed-size blocks on disk; a block read costs milliseconds against nanoseconds for CPU work.
DBMS cost is counted in block accesses.
Records are organised as a heap, sequential or hashed; variable-length records use slotted pages and buffer management keeps hot blocks in memory.

mat.body:
Sometimes a query is so heavy that you would rather do the work once and keep the answer. A materialised view stores a query’s result so repeated queries are instant, at the cost of keeping it fresh. An ordinary view is only a stored query; a materialised view stores the result as well.

Tuning is the art of making slow things fast: add the right indexes, denormalise hot joins, rewrite slow queries, and use EXPLAIN to see the plan. When something is slow, always look at the plan before you guess.
keynotes: A materialised view stores a query’s result so repeated queries are instant, at the cost of keeping it fresh.
Tuning: add the right indexes, denormalise hot joins and rewrite slow queries.
Use EXPLAIN to see the plan.
